section.heading: 4.3. Curve Sketching
A Real-Life Example
section.paragraph: As we have seen on numerous occasions, the graph of a function is a useful aid for visualizing the function’s properties. From a practical point of view, the graph of a function also gives, at one glance, a complete summary of all the information captured by the function.

Consider, for example, the graph of the function giving the Dow-Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) on Black Monday, October 19, 1987 (Figure 44). Here, $$t = 0$$ corresponds to 9:30 a.m., when the market was open for business, and $$t = 6.5$$ corresponds to 4 p.m., the closing time. The following information may be gleaned from studying the graph.

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t is marked from 0 to 7 hours in increments 1 hour. The y axis labeled DJIA is marked from 1700 to 2200 in increments of 100. There is an axis breaker in between 0 and 1700. The curve begins at a marked point (0, 2164), descends downward to the right, concave up, reaches a low point at the marked point (1, 2047), rises upward to the right till approximately (1.5, 2100) where it inflects. From here, the curve rises upward to the right, concave down, reaches a high point at the marked point(2, 2150) and then descends till about (3, 2090) where it inflects again and then descends downward concave up. The curve then reaches a low point at a marked point (4, 2006), levels out and runs parallel to the horizontal axis till (5, 2006), and then descends downward, concave down till the marked point (6.5, 1739).

figure.caption: The Dow-Jones Industrial Average on Black Monday

section.paragraph: The graph is falling rapidly from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 1$$ , reflecting the sharp drop in the index in the first hour of trading. The point $$\left( {1,2047} \right)$$ is a relative minimum point of the function, and this turning point coincides with the start of an aborted recovery. The short-lived rally, represented by the portion of the graph that is rising on the interval $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ , quickly fizzled out at $$t = 2$$ (11:30 a.m.). The relative maximum point $$\left( {2,2150} \right)$$ marks the highest point of the recovery. The function is decreasing in the rest of the interval. The point $$\left( {4,2006} \right)$$ is an inflection point of the function; it shows that there was a temporary respite at $$t = 4$$ (1:30 p.m.). However, selling pressure continued unabated, and the DJIA continued to fall until the closing bell. Finally, the graph also shows that the index opened at the high of the day [ $$f(0) = 2164$$ is the absolute maximum of the function] and closed at the low of the day [ $$f\left( \frac{13}{2} \right) = 1739$$ is the absolute minimum of the function], a drop of $$508$$ points from the previous close!*
Absolute maxima and absolute minima of functions are covered in Section 4.4.
Before we turn our attention to the actual task of sketching the graph of a function, let’s look at some properties of graphs that will be helpful in this connection.
section.heading: Vertical Asymptotes
section.paragraph: Before going on, you might want to review the material on one-sided limits and the limit at infinity of a function (Section 2.4 and 2.5).
Consider the graph of the function
shown in Figure 45. Observe that $$f(x)$$ increases without bound (tends to infinity) as $$x$$ approaches $$x = 1$$ from the right; that is,
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}\frac{x + 1}{x - 1} = \infty$$

figure.caption: The graph of $$f$$ has a vertical asymptote at $$x = 1$$ .

section.paragraph: You can verify this by taking a sequence of values of $$x$$ approaching $$x = 1$$ from the right and looking at the corresponding values of $$f(x)$$ .

Here is another way of looking at the situation: Observe that if $$x$$ is a number that is a little larger than $$1$$ , then both $$\left( {x + 1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ are positive, so $$\left( {x + 1} \right) \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)$$ is also positive. As $$x$$ approaches $$x = 1$$ , the numerator $$\left( {x + 1} \right)$$ approaches the number $$2$$ , but the denominator $$\left( {x - 1} \right)$$ approaches zero, so the quotient $$\left( {x + 1} \right) \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)$$ approaches infinity, as observed earlier. The line $$x = 1$$ is called a vertical asymptote of the graph of $$f$$ .
For the function $$f(x) = {(x + 1) \slash (x - 1)}$$ , you can show that
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}\frac{x + 1}{x - 1} = - \infty$$
and this tells us how $$f(x)$$ approaches the asymptote $$x = 1$$ from the left.
More generally, we have the following definition:

section.paragraph: We next state an important property of polynomial functions.
The graph of a polynomial function has no vertical or horizontal asymptotes.
To see this, note that a polynomial function $$P(x)$$ can be written as a rational function with denominator equal to $$1$$ . Thus,
Since the denominator is never equal to zero, $$P$$ has no vertical asymptotes. Next, if $$P$$ is a polynomial of degree greater than or equal to $$1$$ , then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}P(x)$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}P(x)$$
are either infinity or minus infinity; that is, they do not exist. Therefore, $$P$$ has no horizontal asymptotes.

In Section 4.1 and 4.2, we saw how the first and second derivatives of a function are used to reveal various properties of the graph of a function $$f$$ . We now show how this information can be used to help us sketch the graph of $$f$$ . We begin by giving a general procedure for curve sketching.

list.item: Determine the domain of $$f$$ .

Find the $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -intercepts of $$f$$ .* The equation $$f(x) = 0$$ may be difficult to solve, in which case one may decide against finding the $$x$$ -intercepts or to use technology, if available, for assistance.
Determine the behavior of $$f$$ for large absolute values of $$x$$ .
Find all horizontal and vertical asymptotes of the graph of $$f$$ .
Determine the intervals where $$f$$ is increasing and where $$f$$ is decreasing.
Find the relative extrema of $$f$$ .
Determine the concavity of the graph of $$f$$ .
Find the inflection points of $$f$$ .
Plot a few additional points to help further identify the shape of the graph of $$f$$ and sketch the graph.

section.heading: Using Technology Analyzing the Properties of a Function
section.paragraph: One of the main purposes of studying Section 4.3 is to see how the many concepts of calculus come together to paint a picture of a function. The techniques of graphing also play a very practical role. For example, using the techniques of graphing developed in Section 4.3, you can tell whether the graph of a function generated by a graphing utility is reasonably complete. Furthermore, these techniques can often reveal details that are missing from a graph.

section.heading: Finding x -Intercepts
section.paragraph: As was noted in Section 4.3, it is not always easy to find the $$x$$ -intercepts of the graph of a function. But this information is very important in applications. By using the function for solving polynomial equations or the function for finding the roots of an equation, we can solve the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ quite easily and hence yield the $$x$$ -intercepts of the graph of a function.

list.item: Use the function for solving polynomial equations on a graphing utility to find the $$x$$ -intercepts of the graph of $$f$$ .
Use the function for finding the roots of an equation on a graphing utility to find the $$x$$ -intercepts of the graph of $$f$$ .

Observe that $$f$$ is a polynomial function of degree $$3$$ , and so we may use the function for solving polynomial equations to solve the equation $$x^{3} - 3x^{2} + x + 1.5 = 0\lbrack{f(x) = 0\rbrack}$$ . We find that the solutions ( $$x$$ -intercepts) are $$x_{1} \approx - 0.525687120865 x_{2} \approx 1.2586520225 x_{3} \approx 2.26703509836$$

Using the graph of $$f$$ (Figure T4), we see that $$x_{1} \approx - 0.5$$ , $$x_{2} \approx 1$$ , and $$x_{3} \approx 2$$ . Using the function for finding the roots of an equation on a graphing utility and these values of $$x$$ as initial guesses, we find $$x_{1} \approx - 0.5256871209 x_{2} \approx 1.2586520225 x_{3} \approx 2.2670350984$$ Figure T4 Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: The function for solving polynomial equations on a graphing utility will solve a polynomial equation $$f(x) = 0$$ , where $$f$$ is a polynomial function. The function for finding the roots of an equation, however, will solve equations $$f(x) = 0$$ even if $$f$$ is not a polynomial.

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The graph of $$N$$ in the window $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,30} \right\rbrack$$ is shown in Figure T5a.

Using the function for finding the intersection of the graphs of $$y_{1} = N(t)$$ and $$y_{2} = 20$$ , we find $$t \approx 2.005$$ (see Figure T5b).
